First Jeff Davis County case and the twenty-first county of the US outbreak; the county already sat under TAHC movement restrictions as a neighbour of the Pecos and Brewster County clusters but had no confirmed case of its own until now; domestic cattle; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are the county seat (Fort Davis); confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 20

First detection of New World screwworm in US wildlife and the sixth Pecos County case; hunter-harvested female elk on a game ranch, confirmed at the ARS Knipling-Bushland lab in Kerrville; TAHC is modifying a previously established infested zone and USDA/TPWD are expanding wildlife surveillance in the area; confirmed per APHIS announcement Oct 21

First Otero County case and the twentieth county of the US outbreak; beef cow near Piñon, NM and New Mexico's fifth case; the NM Livestock Board set a minimum 12.4-mile infested zone around the animal; domestic animal; confirmed same day as the Pecos County elk per APHIS dashboard Oct 21

First Hidalgo County case and the twenty-second county of the US outbreak; New Mexico's fourth affected county and sixth case, in the state's bootheel adjoining the Grant County cluster, an area already inside a designated infested zone; domestic cattle; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are the county seat (Lordsburg); confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 22

First Hudspeth County case and the twenty-third county of the US outbreak; Texas's nineteenth affected county, in the far-west corner of the state where Hudspeth runs from the Rio Grande and the Mexican border north to the New Mexico state line; the county had declared a local state of disaster over the screwworm threat in June but had no confirmed case of its own until now; domestic cattle; one of two Hudspeth cases confirmed the same day; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are the Dell City farming valley in the north of the county (the county seat is Sierra Blanca); confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 23

Second Hudspeth County case, confirmed the same day as the first — a same-day cluster in a county with no prior detection, which is how the Grant County, NM and Val Verde County, TX clusters also opened; domestic cattle; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the first Hudspeth case in the Dell City farming valley so the two pins do not render on top of each other; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 23

First Dona Ana County case and the twenty-fourth county of the US outbreak; New Mexico's fifth affected county and seventh case, extending the state's cluster east from Grant and Hidalgo into the Rio Grande valley above El Paso; Dona Ana holds the Santa Teresa port of entry, the border crossing officials had been preparing to reopen to Mexican livestock imports; domestic cattle; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are the county seat (Las Cruces); confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 24

Second Dona Ana County case and the FIRST ovine (sheep) detection in New Mexico — every one of the state's first seven cases was cattle, a horse or a dog, so this is the outbreak's seventeenth sheep case but New Mexico's first; New Mexico's eighth case; domestic animal, confirmed the same day as the Dona Ana cattle case; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the first Dona Ana case near the county seat (Las Cruces) so the two pins do not render on top of each other; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 24

First Luna County case and the twenty-fifth county of the US outbreak; New Mexico's sixth affected county and ninth case; domestic cattle, the thirty-second bovine case of the US outbreak; Luna closes the gap in the southwestern New Mexico cluster, sitting directly between Grant County to the west (3 cases since Sep 17, 2 still active) and Dona Ana County to the east (2 cases on Oct 24), so the state's detections now run unbroken along the Mexican border from Hidalgo through Luna to Dona Ana; Luna also holds the Columbus port of entry, which USDA reopened to Mexican cattle imports the same day this case was confirmed — the third crossing restored under the phased reopening, after Douglas, AZ and Santa Teresa, NM; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are the county seat (Deming), about 32 miles north of Columbus and the border; SU:28227:27, SS:12716:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 26

Third Dona Ana County case and New Mexico's tenth case; the sixth canine (dog) detection of the US outbreak and the first dog in Dona Ana, after the county's cattle and sheep cases on Oct 24 — so all three of the county's cases came inside four days and Dona Ana now spans livestock and companion animals; one of five cases confirmed across Oct 27-28, a cluster Border Report summarised as "four dogs and a cat" and the largest two-day run of the outbreak since the June Zavala cluster; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the other Dona Ana cases near the county seat (Las Cruces) so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28251:27, SS:12722:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 27

First El Paso County case and the TWENTY-SIXTH county of the US outbreak; Texas's twentieth affected county and fifty-eighth case, and the seventh canine (dog) detection overall; by far the most populous county the outbreak has reached — about 870,000 people — and the first case in a major metropolitan area rather than ranch country, which is why the Texas Animal Health Commission drew the infested zone across the whole of El Paso County; the dog was in Socorro, Texas per State Rep. Mary Gonzalez, so unlike most cases in this dataset the coordinates are the reported community rather than the county seat; El Paso County wraps the western tip of Texas between Dona Ana County, NM (4 cases, all active) and Ciudad Juarez, so this detection joins the Texas and New Mexico clusters into one continuous band along the Rio Grande; domestic animal; SU:28252:27, SS:12725:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 27

First Cochise County case and the first detection of New World screwworm in ARIZONA — the TWENTY-SEVENTH county and the THIRD STATE of the US outbreak, after Texas and New Mexico, and the first new state since New Mexico's Lea County dog on Jun 7; the eighth canine (dog) detection overall; the dog was on a Cochise County ranch, where a local veterinarian found a maggot-infested wound on its back on Oct 26, and samples were tested and confirmed at the APHIS National Veterinary Services Laboratories in Ames, Iowa on Oct 28; APHIS and the Arizona Department of Agriculture are running a joint response under the APHIS NWS Response Playbook: a 20-km infested zone around the detection, animal movement controls for that area, increased live animal surveillance and trapping, sterile fly releases (roughly a million flies released in the Cochise County area) and targeted outreach to producers, veterinarians and communities, with other livestock on the ranch being evaluated; Cochise County borders Hidalgo County, NM (1 active case) to the east, so Arizona's first detection is contiguous with the existing southwestern New Mexico cluster rather than a long-range jump; Cochise also holds the Douglas port of entry — the FIRST crossing USDA reopened to Mexican cattle imports under the phased reopening, ahead of Santa Teresa, NM and Columbus, NM — and is the planned site of Arizona's sterile fly facility; APHIS has not disclosed the location within the county, so the coordinates are the county seat (Bisbee); SU:28258:27, SS:12741:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard and APHIS announcement Oct 28

Fourth Dona Ana County case and New Mexico's eleventh case; the ninth canine (dog) detection of the US outbreak and the county's second dog on consecutive days, after case 68 on Oct 27; Dona Ana is now the outbreak's LARGEST ACTIVE cluster, with 4 cases all active across cattle, sheep and two dogs, all confirmed inside five days — more active cases than any other county, though Crockett County, TX is still the largest cluster by total cases at 13, all of them long since closed; and Las Cruces sits inside the resulting infested zone; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the other Dona Ana cases near the county seat (Las Cruces) so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28277:27, SS:12742:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 28

FIRST FELINE (CAT) DETECTION OF THE US OUTBREAK — a domestic cat, and the seventh species the outbreak has infected after cattle, sheep, goats, dogs, horses and one elk; APHIS records the species as "Domestic Cat"; fourth Grant County case and New Mexico's twelfth case, which makes Grant the state's joint-largest cluster alongside Dona Ana at 4 cases each; Grant's cases now run horse (Sep 17, inactive), cattle and horse (Oct 15, both active) and this cat, so 3 of its 4 are active; a cat is a second companion-animal species after dogs and, like the dog cases, it points to the fly being established in the local environment rather than moving with livestock shipments — cats are not transported under livestock permits and are not covered by the movement controls the response relies on; one of five cases confirmed across Oct 27-28, the cluster Border Report summarised as "four dogs and a cat"; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the other Grant cases near the county seat (Silver City) so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28278:27, SS:12743:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 28

Second Presidio County case and Texas's fifty-ninth case; the thirty-third bovine (cattle) detection of the US outbreak; this case was absent from the daily brief and was found by diffing the APHIS case-level export, which is also why it carries a later id than the Oct 28 cases the previous sync recorded despite a lower APHIS reference. Presidio's only earlier case was the Sep 9 ranch horse — the FIRST EQUINE case of the US outbreak — which has since gone inactive, so this is the county's first active case in seven weeks and its first in livestock. Presidio is the Big Bend border county on the Rio Grande opposite Ojinaga, Chihuahua, and it sits between Brewster County to the east (6 cases, 1 active) and Jeff Davis County to the north (1 active), so this detection fills in the middle of the Big Bend cluster rather than opening new ground — no new county, the outbreak stays at 27. The Texas Animal Health Commission issued a modified Executive Director Order for Jeff Davis and Presidio Counties on Oct 29, the day after confirmation, and both counties remain under animal movement restrictions. Texas's active count rises from 7 to 8 with this case; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the Sep 9 horse case near the city of Presidio so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28275:27, SS:12744:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 28

Fifth Dona Ana County case and New Mexico's thirteenth case; the thirty-fourth bovine (cattle) detection of the US outbreak and the county's second head of cattle, after the Oct 24 cow. Dona Ana is now the outbreak's LARGEST ACTIVE CLUSTER outright, with 5 cases all active — 2 cattle, 1 sheep and 2 dogs — and it also passes Grant County to become New Mexico's largest cluster by total cases; Crockett County, TX is still the largest cluster by total cases overall at 13, though all 13 are long since closed. All five Dona Ana cases landed inside six days: two on Oct 24, then a two-day gap across Oct 25 and Oct 26, then one each on Oct 27, Oct 28 and Oct 29 — a three-day unbroken run. The county spans livestock and companion animals, and Las Cruces and the New Mexico State University campus both fall inside the resulting 12.4-mile infested zone; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the other Dona Ana cases near the county seat (Las Cruces) so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28285:27, SS:12752:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 29

Second Luna County case and New Mexico's fourteenth case; the thirty-fifth bovine (cattle) detection of the US outbreak; this case was absent from the daily brief and was found by diffing the APHIS case-level export. Both of Luna's cases are cattle and both are active, three days apart — the county's first was Oct 26, which opened Luna as the twenty-fifth county of the outbreak. Luna sits directly between Grant County to the northwest (4 cases, 3 active) and Dona Ana County to the east (5 cases, all active), so New Mexico's detections still run unbroken along the Mexican border from Hidalgo through Luna to Dona Ana, and the two counties either side of Luna are now the state's two largest clusters. Luna also holds the Columbus port of entry, the third crossing USDA restored to Mexican cattle imports under the phased reopening, after Douglas, AZ and Santa Teresa, NM; this second case comes three days after that reopening. Confirmed the same day as the Dona Ana cow, taking New Mexico to 12 of the outbreak's 21 active cases — more than Texas (8) and Arizona (1) combined; domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the Oct 26 case near the county seat (Deming), about 32 miles north of Columbus and the border; SU:28286:27, SS:12753:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 29

Sixth Dona Ana County case and New Mexico's fifteenth case; the TENTH CANINE (dog) detection of the US outbreak and the county's THIRD DOG IN FOUR DAYS, after the Oct 27 dog (case 68) and the Oct 28 dog (case 71). Dona Ana remains the outbreak's LARGEST ACTIVE CLUSTER and widens its lead to a factor of two: 6 cases, all active, across three species — 2 cattle, 1 sheep and 3 dogs — against Grant County, NM at 3 active. It is also New Mexico's largest cluster by total cases, ahead of Grant at 4; Crockett County, TX is still the largest cluster by total cases overall at 13, though all 13 are long since closed. All six Dona Ana cases landed inside seven days: two on Oct 24, a two-day gap across Oct 25 and Oct 26, then one each on Oct 27, Oct 28, Oct 29 and Oct 30 — a four-day unbroken run. Half the cluster is now dogs, and dogs move outside the livestock permit system the response depends on, so a third canine detection in four days in one county points to the fly breeding locally rather than arriving with shipments; APHIS also confirmed a WILD FLY TRAP detection in Dona Ana County on Oct 29 (SU:28266:27), the first in New Mexico, which is independent evidence of the same thing — fly-trap detections are not animal cases and are not counted in this tracker. Las Cruces and the New Mexico State University campus both fall inside the resulting 12.4-mile infested zone. New Mexico now holds 13 of the outbreak's 22 active cases, more than Texas (8) and Arizona (1) combined. Domestic animal; APHIS reports location at county level, so the coordinates are offset slightly from the other five Dona Ana cases near the county seat (Las Cruces) so the pins do not render on top of each other; SU:28348:27, SS:12774:27; confirmed per APHIS dashboard Oct 30

Case 52: goat in Crockett County — thirteenth Crockett County case; US total reaches 51 with 3 active cases (50 Presidio horse, 51 Grant NM horse, 52 Crockett goat)
Case 50 (Presidio County horse, confirmed Sep 9) moved to inactive per the APHIS dashboard. No new domestic cases; US total holds at 51 with 2 active (51 Grant NM horse, 52 Crockett goat)

Case 53: dog in Brewster County, TX — fifth Brewster County case and fifth canine detection of the US outbreak (fourth in Texas); US total reaches 52 domestic animal cases with 3 active (51 Grant NM horse, 52 Crockett goat, 53 Brewster dog)

APHIS reconciliation: the dashboard's 53 headline is 52 domestic animal cases plus the Sep 25 Brewster County fly-trap detection, which APHIS counts under total cases but not under domestic animal cases. No un-ingested animal case; tracker at 52 with 3 active

Case 51 (Grant County, NM horse, confirmed Sep 17) moved to inactive per the APHIS dashboard — 21 days after confirmation, matching the outbreak's typical resolution window. No new domestic cases; US total holds at 52 domestic animal cases with 2 active (52 Crockett goat, 53 Brewster dog). New Mexico has no active cases for the first time since the Grant County detection

Case 54: cattle in Pecos County, TX — fifth Pecos County case and the first bovine detection in that county, which had previously recorded only sheep and a dog. US total reaches 53 domestic animal cases

Cases 55 and 56: cattle and a horse confirmed the same day in Grant County, NM — the first bovine case in New Mexico and the third equine detection of the US outbreak. New Mexico rises to 4 cases (Lea dog, Grant horse Sep 17, Grant cattle Oct 15, Grant horse Oct 15) with 2 active. US total reaches 55 domestic animal cases; no new county or state, holding at 19 counties across 2 states

Case 57: horse in Brewster County, TX — sixth Brewster County case and the fourth equine detection of the US outbreak, the second in Texas after the Sep 9 Presidio County horse. Brewster becomes the second-heaviest county in the outbreak behind Crockett (13), and Texas rises to 52 cases. US total reaches 56 domestic animal cases with 5 active and 51 inactive; no new county or state, holding at 19 counties across 2 states. All 5 active cases are October detections

Case 52 (Crockett County, TX goat, confirmed Sep 26) moved to inactive per the APHIS dashboard, clearing September of active cases — all 4 remaining active cases are now October detections (53 Brewster dog, 54 Pecos cattle, 55 Grant cattle, 56 Grant horse). US total stands at 55 domestic animal cases with 4 active and 51 inactive

Case 60: cattle in Val Verde County, TX — the county's third case and its first bovine detection. Val Verde had been quiet since its Aug 16 sheep and Aug 25 goat, both of which were reclassified inactive on Sep 13, so this is its first active case in five weeks and marks the outbreak re-appearing in the Del Rio border corridor while the western clusters expand

Case 61: cattle in Jeff Davis County, TX — the first case in Jeff Davis County, which becomes the twenty-first county of the US outbreak. The county was already under Texas Animal Health Commission movement restrictions as a neighbour of the Pecos and Brewster County clusters but had never recorded a confirmed case; Texas rises to 55 cases across 19 counties

Case 58: hunter-harvested female elk in Pecos County, TX — the first detection of New World screwworm in US wildlife. The hunter reported the animal on a game ranch and the sample was confirmed at the ARS Knipling-Bushland U.S. Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville. Cervid becomes the sixth species of the outbreak and the first that is neither livestock nor a companion animal; Pecos County rises to 6 cases and Texas to 53. The Texas Animal Health Commission is modifying a previously established infested zone while USDA and Texas Parks and Wildlife expand wildlife surveillance in the area

Case 59: beef cow in Otero County, NM — the first case in Otero County, which becomes the twentieth county of the US outbreak, confirmed the same day as the Pecos County elk. New Mexico rises to 5 cases and the New Mexico Livestock Board established a minimum 12.4-mile infested zone around the affected animal near Piñon. US total reaches 58 animal cases with 7 active and 51 inactive across 20 counties in 2 states; 57 of the 58 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife

Case 62: cattle in Hidalgo County, NM — the first case in Hidalgo County, which becomes the twenty-second county of the US outbreak and New Mexico's fourth affected county. The detection is in the state's bootheel, adjoining the Grant County cluster and inside territory New Mexico had already designated an infested zone; New Mexico rises to 6 cases. US total reaches 61 animal cases with 9 active and 52 inactive across 22 counties in 2 states; 60 of the 61 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife

Case 58, the Pecos County elk and the outbreak's only wildlife detection, is reclassified from active to inactive per the APHIS dashboard — the first October case to be closed out, one day after it was confirmed. Pecos County drops to a single active case and all 9 remaining active cases are domestic animals

Cases 63 and 64: two cattle confirmed the same day in Hudspeth County, TX — the first cases in Hudspeth County, which becomes the twenty-third county of the US outbreak and Texas's nineteenth affected county. Hudspeth is in the far-west corner of the state, running from the Rio Grande and the Mexican border north to the New Mexico line, and had declared a local state of disaster over the screwworm threat back in June without ever recording a case of its own. The pair opens the county with a same-day cluster and pushes the outbreak roughly 150 miles northwest of the Jeff Davis and Pecos clusters, into the corridor between the Texas and New Mexico detections; Texas rises to 57 cases

Case 65: cattle in Dona Ana County, NM — the first case in Dona Ana County, which becomes the twenty-fourth county of the US outbreak and New Mexico's fifth affected county. The detection extends the New Mexico cluster east from Grant and Hidalgo into the Rio Grande valley above El Paso, and Dona Ana holds the Santa Teresa port of entry — the border crossing state and federal officials had been preparing to reopen to Mexican livestock imports

Case 66: sheep in Dona Ana County, NM — the first ovine detection in New Mexico, confirmed the same day as the Dona Ana cattle case. Every one of New Mexico's first seven cases was cattle, a horse or a dog, so although this is the seventeenth sheep case of the US outbreak it is the state's first, and it widens the species profile of the New Mexico cluster beyond cattle for the first time since the Grant County horses. New Mexico rises to 8 cases across 5 counties, 6 of them active. US total reaches 65 animal cases with 12 active and 53 inactive across 24 counties in 2 states; 64 of the 65 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife

Case 53, the Oct 2 Brewster County dog, is reclassified from active to inactive per the APHIS dashboard — the first of October's domestic cases to be closed out, and the only domestic inactive case the month has recorded. Brewster County drops to a single active case. All 12 remaining active cases are domestic animals and all are October detections, split 6 in Texas and 6 in New Mexico — the first time New Mexico, with 8 cases to Texas's 57, has carried half the outbreak's active caseload

Case 67: cattle in Luna County, NM — the first case in Luna County, which becomes the twenty-fifth county of the US outbreak and New Mexico's sixth affected county. Luna closes the gap in the southwestern New Mexico cluster: it is bordered by Grant and Hidalgo to the west and Dona Ana to the east, so with this detection New Mexico's cases run unbroken along the Mexican border from Hidalgo through Luna to Dona Ana. The case was confirmed the same day USDA reopened the Columbus port of entry, in Luna County, to Mexican cattle imports — the third crossing restored under the phased reopening after Douglas, AZ and Santa Teresa, NM, and a route that normally carries a large share of the Mexican cattle entering the US. New Mexico rises to 9 cases across 6 counties, 7 of them active, which puts the state ahead of Texas on active cases for the first time in the outbreak — Texas holds 57 cases but only 6 active. US total reaches 66 animal cases with 13 active and 53 inactive across 25 counties in 2 states; 65 of the 66 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife

Cases 68 and 69: a dog in Dona Ana County, NM and a dog in El Paso County, TX. El Paso is the first case in the county and the twenty-sixth county of the US outbreak — Texas's twentieth affected county, its fifty-eighth case, and by far the most populous county the outbreak has reached at about 870,000 people. It is the first detection in a major metropolitan area rather than ranch country, and the Texas Animal Health Commission responded by drawing an infested zone across the whole of El Paso County; the dog was in Socorro, Texas. Because El Paso County wraps the western tip of Texas between Dona Ana County, NM and Ciudad Juarez, the Texas and New Mexico clusters are now one continuous band along the Rio Grande. The Dona Ana dog is the county's third case in four days, after cattle and sheep on Oct 24, and New Mexico's tenth case. Both are dogs, the outbreak's sixth and seventh canine detections

ARIZONA BECOMES THE THIRD STATE. Case 70: a dog on a ranch in Cochise County, AZ — the first detection of New World screwworm in Arizona, the twenty-seventh county of the US outbreak, and the first new state since New Mexico's Lea County dog on Jun 7. A local veterinarian found a maggot-infested wound on the dog's back on Oct 26 and APHIS confirmed the sample at the National Veterinary Services Laboratories in Ames, Iowa. APHIS and the Arizona Department of Agriculture opened a joint response under the APHIS NWS Response Playbook: a 20-km infested zone around the detection, animal movement controls, increased live animal surveillance and trapping, sterile fly releases — about a million flies in the Cochise County area — and targeted outreach. Cochise borders Hidalgo County, NM, so Arizona's first case is contiguous with the southwestern New Mexico cluster rather than a long-range jump; it also holds the Douglas port of entry, the first crossing USDA reopened to Mexican cattle, and the planned site of Arizona's sterile fly facility. Two more New Mexico cases landed the same day: case 71, a second Dona Ana dog on consecutive days, and case 72, a DOMESTIC CAT in Grant County — the outbreak's FIRST FELINE DETECTION and its seventh species after cattle, sheep, goats, dogs, horses and one elk. Cats move outside the livestock permit system the response depends on, so like the dog cases the detection points to the fly being established locally rather than travelling with shipments. Five cases were confirmed across Oct 27-28 — four dogs and a cat, the outbreak's largest two-day run since June. US total reaches 71 animal cases with 18 active and 53 inactive across 27 counties in 3 states; 70 of the 71 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife. New Mexico leads on active cases with 10 of the 18, from 12 cases across 6 counties, against Texas's 7 active from 58 cases and Arizona's 1

Case 73: cattle in Presidio County, TX — the county's second case and its first in livestock, after the Sep 9 ranch horse that was the outbreak's first equine detection. Picked up from the APHIS case-level export rather than any announcement; the Texas Animal Health Commission issued a modified Executive Director Order for Jeff Davis and Presidio Counties the following day. Presidio sits between Brewster and Jeff Davis on the Rio Grande, so the Big Bend cluster fills in rather than spreading — the outbreak stays at 27 counties in 3 states.

Cases 74 and 75: cattle in Dona Ana County, NM and cattle in Luna County, NM. Dona Ana's fifth case makes it the outbreak's largest active cluster outright — 5 cases, all active, across 2 cattle, 1 sheep and 2 dogs — and New Mexico's largest cluster by total cases, passing Grant. Luna takes its second case three days after its first. The outbreak reaches 74 animal cases with 21 active, and New Mexico now holds 12 of those 21 actives, more than Texas (8) and Arizona (1) combined, having had just 5 cases in total two weeks earlier.

Case 76: a dog in Dona Ana County, NM — the county's sixth case in seven days and its THIRD DOG IN FOUR DAYS, after the dogs of Oct 27 and Oct 28, and the tenth canine detection of the US outbreak. Dona Ana now holds 6 cases, all active, across three species (2 cattle, 1 sheep, 3 dogs), which doubles its lead as the outbreak's largest active cluster over Grant County, NM at 3. Half the cluster is dogs, which move outside the livestock permit system the response is built around; APHIS also confirmed the first WILD FLY TRAP detection in New Mexico in the same county on Oct 29, so both lines of evidence now point to the fly breeding locally around Las Cruces rather than arriving with shipments. The outbreak reaches 75 animal cases with 22 active and 53 inactive across 27 counties in 3 states; 74 of the 75 are domestic animals and 1 is wildlife. New Mexico holds 13 of the 22 actives from 15 cases across 6 counties — more than Texas (8 active from 59 cases) and Arizona (1) combined.
